_metadata.method: partner arm: pool UniProt curated interaction partners of known autoantigens (epitope-spreading prior); filter hubs (specificity>=min) and thin annotation (degree>=min); rank by support (# known antigens linked), then specificity, then the nuclear/NA prior. specificity = links-to-known-antigens / total partners.
_metadata.framing: Candidates are CITED HYPOTHESES for expert review, not confirmed discoveries.
_metadata.caveat: Partner arm finds complex-members well; standalone antigens (e.g. Ro60, no curated interactions) are invisible to it — a known coverage gap. Specificity controls for hub bias (e.g. HTT, 860 partners, correctly demoted).

ranking.order: support, then specificity, then nuclear/NA prior
ranking.note: Transparent multi-signal ranking; filters/order are a documented first pass.

agent_assessments.transcript:
## Assessment: Is SF3A2 (Q15428) an SLE autoantigen?

**What the protein is (UniProt):** SF3A2 / "Splicing factor 3A subunit 2" (SAP62) is a component of the SF3A subcomplex (SF3A1/SF3A2/SF3A3) of the **17S U2 snRNP** of the spliceosome. It associates with U2 snRNP and spliceosome complexes but is a **U2-specific** splicing factor, not itself one of the Sm core proteins. (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q15428/entry)

**Structural confidence (AlphaFold):** Mean pLDDT 64.1/100 — a **Low** confidence band, so the predicted 3D model is not reliable overall. (https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/Q15428)

**Literature on autoantigen status:** I ran five targeted searches (`SF3A2 autoantibody autoantigen lupus`, `SF3A2/SAP62 autoantibody autoimmune`, `SF3A splicing factor autoantibody SLE`, `anti-SF3A2 antibody disease`, `U2 snRNP anti-U2-RNP autoantibody`). None returned any paper reporting SF3A2 (or anti-U2 SF3A) as a target of autoantibodies:
- SF3A2-specific hits were all **cancer biology, splicing mechanism, or cardiac** papers, not autoimmunity (e.g., colorectal cancer biomarker, https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41399366; myocardial I/R splicing, https://europepmc.org/article/MED/38101749).
- The U2/autoantibody search returned only general SLE/scleroderma antibody reviews (e.g., anti-Sm in SLE classification, https://europepmc.org/article/MED/35464346; autoantigen RNP review, https://europepmc.org/article/MED/33722441) — none implicating SF3A2.

**Interpretation (for your review):** Your premise is supported — SF3A2 does belong to the U2 snRNP machinery that neighbors the Sm core and U1-C. However, SF3A2 is a *U2-specific interacting/structural* subunit, **not** itself a Sm-core protein, and there is no named clinical antibody test (e.g., anti-Sm, anti-U1-RNP) that captures it. Under the stated judging rule, "merely interacting with" an autoantigen complex does not confer autoantigen status. Critically, the tools surfaced **no published evidence** that SF3A2 is targeted by autoantibodies in SLE or any related autoimmune disease.

Caveat: absence of evidence in these searches is not proof it has never been reported; a specialist proteomic autoantigen database (outside my tools) could be checked as a next step.

EVIDENCE: NONE-FOUND

## Assessment: Is CLNS1A (P54105) an SLE autoantigen?

**Protein identity & relationship to known autoantigens**
CLNS1A encodes the methylosome subunit pICln, a chaperone that regulates assembly of spliceosomal snRNPs. In the cytosol it traps Sm proteins (SNRPD1/D2, SNRPE/F/G) in an inactive 6S pICln-Sm complex, and it is a component of the 20S methylosome (with PRMT5 and WDR77) [UniProt: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P54105/entry]. Importantly, the 6S pICln-Sm complex is described as a "ring-like structure where CLNS1A/pICln *mimics* additional Sm proteins and which is *unable to assemble into the core snRNP*" [UniProt, same source]. So pICln is an **assembly chaperone that transiently associates** with Sm proteins — it is *not* itself a chain of the mature Sm core / snRNP particle that anti-Sm antibodies capture.

**Structural confidence (context only)**
AlphaFold mean pLDDT = 75.5 ("Confident" band) [AlphaFold: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/P54105].

**Literature search for autoantigen/autoantibody evidence**
I ran five searches combining the gene (CLNS1A), the protein name (pICln), the methylosome, and SLE/anti-Sm/autoantibody terms. None returned a paper reporting that CLNS1A/pICln is targeted by autoantibodies or is an autoantigen:
- "CLNS1A autoantibody autoantigen lupus" → no results.
- "pICln autoantibody systemic lupus erythematosus" → only tangential hits (Sm/LSm4 dimethylation; EJC factor Y14) [e.g., https://europepmc.org/article/MED/11720283], neither about pICln as an autoantibody target.
- "methylosome pICln autoantigen autoimmune" → off-topic (retinal vascular disease) [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/22982179].
- "CLNS1A anti-Sm antibody target" → PRMT5/splicing and cancer papers; notably "CLNS1A regulates genome stability and cell cycle progression to control CD4 T cell function and autoimmunity" (2025) [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/40540585] — this implicates CLNS1A in T-cell *function* and autoimmunity mechanistically, but does **not** report CLNS1A as a target of autoantibodies.
- "pICln chloride channel autoantibody disease" → off-topic (reproductive sciences) [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/32030671].

**Interpretation (for your review)**
- No tool-returned evidence shows CLNS1A/pICln is itself bound by SLE autoantibodies.
- Under the stated rules, CLNS1A does **not** qualify as an established autoantigen by complex-membership: it is a transient chaperone that *mimics/interacts with* Sm proteins but is explicitly not part of the assembled Sm-core snRNP captured by anti-Sm testing — so the "merely interacts with" exclusion applies.
- The one autoimmunity-linked paper concerns a functional/regulatory role in CD4 T cells, not autoantigenicity. That is a different kind of claim and should not be read as autoantibody evidence.

A reasonable next step, if you want to be exhaustive, would be a proteomics-focused search (e.g., autoantigen discovery / immunoprecipitation screens) or checking the specific 2025 T-cell paper's full text — but based on the tools, no autoantibody/autoantigen report exists.

EVIDENCE: NONE-FOUND

## Assessment: Is FUBP1 a published SLE autoantigen?

**Protein identity (UniProt).** FUBP1 = Far upstream element-binding protein 1 (gene FUBP1, accession Q96AE4), a 644-aa transcription regulator of MYC that binds the single-stranded FUSE element; documented to form a complex with PUF60 and the FUSE DNA segment and to interact with PUF60 and JTV1. Notably, the UniProt record does **not** list any interaction with Sm-B/B', U1-A, or U1-C — so the snRNP associations stated in your prompt are not corroborated by the tool. Source: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q96AE4/entry

**Structure confidence (AlphaFold).** Mean pLDDT 63.6/100 — "Low" confidence overall (consistent with a protein containing flexible/disordered single-stranded-nucleic-acid-binding regions). Source: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/Q96AE4

**Literature findings.**
- **Direct autoantibody evidence, but in cancer, not autoimmunity:** Circulating autoantibodies to FUBP1 (alongside ENO1) were reported as negative prognostic markers in pancreatic cancer — demonstrating FUBP1 *can* be an autoantibody target, though in an oncologic rather than SLE/autoimmune context. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37910256
- **Catalog/candidate listings:** FUBP1 surfaces in the "master autoantigen-ome" work linking alternative splicing and autoimmune disease, and in a B-lymphoblast autoantigen-ome (Wang/Roehrl et al., 2021–2022). These are broad proteomic candidate-autoantigen catalogs rather than disease-specific validations. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/35237749 ; https://europepmc.org/article/PPR/PPR307555 ; https://europepmc.org/article/PPR/PPR378369
- **Occult autoimmunity antibody profiling:** An INSPIRE-trial antibody-profiling paper (2026) appears in these searches but is not demonstrably FUBP1-/SLE-specific from the retrieved metadata. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41559617

**Interpretation (for your review).** FUBP1 is *not* a core component of any recognized SLE autoantigen complex (Sm core/snRNP, U1-RNP, nucleosome, ribosomal P, Ku, Ro/La) in the tool evidence — it only interacts with transcription/splicing partners — so the "established by complex membership" criterion does not apply. There is published evidence that FUBP1 can be targeted by autoantibodies (clearest in pancreatic cancer) and that it appears in candidate autoantigen catalogs touching autoimmunity, but I found **no tool-sourced paper establishing FUBP1 as a validated SLE (or defined autoimmune-disease) autoantigen** with a named clinical antibody test. The evidence is suggestive but thin and largely cross-disease. An expert may wish to open the autoantigen-ome and INSPIRE papers directly to confirm whether FUBP1 is explicitly tied to SLE patient sera.

EVIDENCE: EMERGING

## Assessment: Is C1QBP an SLE autoantigen?

**Protein identity (UniProt):** C1QBP (Q07021) is "Complement component 1 Q subcomponent-binding protein, mitochondrial," a 282-aa protein (also known as gC1qR / p32 / HABP1). The UniProt record documents roles in microbial infection (Rubella replication, EBNA1 interaction) but lists **no autoantigen/autoimmune function**. Source: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q07021/entry

**Structural confidence (AlphaFold):** Mean pLDDT 75.1/100 — "Confident" band. This speaks only to model reliability, not to any disease role. Source: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/Q07021

**Literature search (Europe PMC):** I ran seven searches across the protein's multiple names (C1QBP, gC1qR, p32, HABP1) and several diseases (SLE, lupus nephritis, Sjögren's, RA, hereditary angioedema, vasculitis), using explicit "autoantibody"/"autoantigen" terms. **None returned a paper reporting that C1QBP itself is bound by autoantibodies or serves as an autoantigen in SLE or a related autoimmune disease.** Returned hits were either general reviews (e.g., mitochondria in rheumatic disease, https://europepmc.org/article/MED/36175664) or concerned C1q itself rather than its binding protein (e.g., "Anti-DNA antibodies cross-react with C1q," https://europepmc.org/article/MED/23834843). One COVID-19 autoantigen-profiling paper appeared (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/33971585) but it is not SLE-focused and I found no tool evidence that C1QBP specifically features in it.

**Interpretation (for your review):** Your premise — that C1QBP physically associates with the known SLE autoantigens C1q A/B/C — is a reasonable basis for interest. However, under the rules I follow, a *binding partner/interactor* of an autoantigen complex is **not** itself an established autoantigen unless there is direct evidence. The named clinical anti-C1q test targets C1q, not its binding protein. I found **no published evidence** that C1QBP is an antibody target in SLE or related autoimmune disease. This is a negative-search result, not proof of absence; a specialist could check sources my tools don't index (e.g., proteomic autoantigen arrays, conference abstracts).

EVIDENCE: NONE-FOUND

## Assessment: GIGYF1 (O75420) as a potential SLE autoantigen

**Protein identity (confirmed):** GIGYF1 is "GRB10-interacting GYF protein 1," 1035 aa, whose documented function is regulating tyrosine kinase receptor (IGF1R) signaling together with GRB10, and it interacts with DDX6. UniProt's listed binding partners are GRB10 and DDX6 — **no snRNP/Sm/U1 components are recorded in the UniProt subunit data** (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/O75420/entry). So the premise that it associates with Sm-B/B', U1-A and U1-C is not something my tools could confirm.

**Structural confidence:** AlphaFold gives a mean pLDDT of 55.2/100 — "Low" confidence, consistent with a largely disordered/flexible protein; the predicted 3D model should be treated cautiously (https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/O75420).

**Literature on autoantigen/autoantibody status:** I ran five searches (combining GIGYF1/GYF-protein with autoantibody, autoantigen, lupus/SLE, autoimmune disease, and a GIGYF2 cross-check). None returned any paper describing GIGYF1 (or GIGYF2) as a target of autoantibodies or as an autoantigen in SLE or any related disease. The only autoimmune-adjacent hits were **genetic association / GWAS or rare-variant studies** (e.g., GIGYF1 loss-of-function and type 2 diabetes, https://europepmc.org/article/MED/34732801; Hashimoto's thyroiditis GWAS, https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42527560; autoimmune thyroid disease susceptibility, https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37197658). These concern DNA-level susceptibility, **not** the protein being targeted by autoantibodies — a different kind of evidence.

**Bottom line (for your review):** My tools found no published evidence that GIGYF1 is itself an autoantibody target or a recognized autoantigen in SLE or related autoimmune disease. Nor could my tools confirm the stated physical association with Sm/U1 snRNP autoantigen components. It therefore reads as a structural/interaction candidate at best, not an established or even emerging autoantigen. Note this is absence of evidence in the sources I queried, not proof of absence — a specialist proteomic/immunoprecipitation database or targeted experimental search could be a sensible next step.

EVIDENCE: NONE-FOUND

## Assessment: Is COIL (Coilin, P38432) an SLE autoantigen?

**Protein identity (UniProt)**
- COIL encodes **Coilin**, a 576-aa structural component of nuclear coiled bodies (Cajal bodies), involved in modification/assembly of nucleoplasmic snRNPs. Documented interactors include SMN1, WRAP53/TCAB1, AK6, and others. [https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P38432/entry]
- Note: The UniProt record I retrieved does **not** list Ku70, Ku80, or Sm-B/B′ among its documented interactors, so I cannot confirm those specific associations from tool evidence.

**Structural confidence (AlphaFold)**
- Mean pLDDT **58.5/100 — "Low"** confidence, consistent with coilin being largely intrinsically disordered. Any structure-based interpretation should be cautious. [https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/P38432]

**Published autoantigen evidence (Europe PMC)**
- **Landmark primary evidence:** Coilin was literally *discovered as a human autoantigen*. Andrade et al. (1991) described a patient autoantibody targeting a novel coiled-body protein and cloned it as **p80-coilin** — "Human autoantibody to a novel protein of the nuclear coiled body: immunological characterization and cDNA cloning of p80-coilin." [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/2033369]
- **Clinical/laboratory recognition:** Anti-coilin produces a recognized nuclear HEp-2 immunofluorescence pattern that is codified in the **International Consensus on Standardized ANA HEp-2 Patterns (ICAP)** nomenclature (Chan et al. 2015). [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/26347739] Related reviews on ANA patterns and their clinical significance reinforce that coiled/Cajal-body (anti-coilin) reactivity is a catalogued ANA specificity. [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42923724]

**Interpretation and caveats (for your review)**
- The tools confirm coilin is a *bona fide*, published autoantibody target — it was identified through patient autoantibodies and has a named ANA pattern. By that measure it is a **recognized autoantigen in systemic autoimmunity**.
- However, my searches did **not** return evidence that anti-coilin is a *specific or characteristic marker of SLE*. It is described as rare and spread across systemic autoimmune conditions rather than defining one disease, and it is **not** a member of the classic SLE autoantigen complexes (Sm/snRNP, nucleosome, ribosomal P, Ku, Ro/La), so the "complex-membership" shortcut for SLE does not apply here.
- Bottom line: coilin's status as an autoantigen is well established in the literature; its specific tie to **SLE** is weak/unclear from the evidence retrieved, and would merit a targeted follow-up (e.g., searching SLE-cohort seroprevalence studies for anti-coilin).

EVIDENCE: ESTABLISHED  -- tools found it is already a recognized autoantigen in the disease
